title: Akshay Kumar's ₹264 Crore Haunted House Just Landed on Netflix. After 14 Years, Priyadarshan Still Knows How to Scare You Laughing.
excerpt: Bhooth Bangla — the Priyadarshan-Akshay reunion that became his third-biggest post-Covid hit — is now streaming worldwide on Netflix in Hindi and English. Here's why the diaspora should clear a weekend.
body:
It opens, as all the best Priyadarshan films do, with a man walking confidently into a place he absolutely should not be. **Akshay Kumar** is Arjun, who inherits an ancestral palace in the cursed village of Mangalpur and — against every warning the locals throw at him — decides it's the perfect venue for a destination wedding. Newlywed brides have a habit of vanishing here, snatched by an immortal demon named Vadhusur. Arjun, naturally, lights the mandap anyway. What follows is two hours and fifty-three minutes of doors slamming on their own, candles guttering, and the particular brand of old-school chaos that only one director in Hindi cinema still knows how to choreograph.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=sL7V1INn6io</youtube>

After a theatrical run that quietly turned into one of the year's better Bollywood stories, **Bhooth Bangla** began streaming on **Netflix** on June 12 — in Hindi and English, available everywhere the platform reaches. For the diaspora, that's the whole point. No region locks, no "available in India only" heartbreak, no waiting for a grey-market upload. If you're in New Jersey or Brampton or Wembley, the haunted house is now in your living room.

And it earned its way there. Against a ₹120 crore budget, the film crossed a worldwide gross of nearly ₹264 crore, riding a genuinely leggy theatrical run that saw it holding screens into its seventh and eighth weeks — a rarity in an era when films evaporate after their opening Friday. It's set to finish as **Akshay Kumar's third-highest post-Covid grosser**, a number that matters for an actor who's spent the last few years searching for the hit that sticks. This one stuck.



> **"No region locks, no "available in India only" heartbreak, no waiting for a grey-market upload."**


## The Reunion That Carried It


![Akshay Kumar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2a/Akshay_Kumar_National_Award_for_Padman_%28cropped%29.jpg)


The real headline isn't the box office. It's the byline. **Bhooth Bangla** marks the reunion of Akshay Kumar and director **Priyadarshan** after fourteen years apart — the pairing that gave us *Hera Pheri*, *Garam Masala*, *Bhagam Bhag*, and a comedy sensibility that defined an entire era of multiplex Bollywood. Watching them back together is like hearing a band that broke up in 2012 play the old songs again. The timing is rusty in places, but the chemistry is muscle memory.

> "BHOOTH BANGLA is a fair entertainer that works best for its humour, performances and old-school Priyadarshan-style chaos." — Bollywood Hungama, 3.5/5

The ensemble is stacked the way Priyadarshan's films always are — **Tabu**, **Paresh Rawal**, **Wamiqa Gabbi**, Mithila Palkar, Rajpal Yadav, Mithun Chakraborty, and what feels like half the comic character actors in the industry crammed into one cursed estate. Pritam scores it; Arijit Singh and Armaan Malik lend the soundtrack. It's maximalist in the way only a Priyadarshan production can be, and that's either the appeal or the exhaustion, depending on your tolerance for a climax that genuinely overstays its welcome.

## The Honest Verdict

The critics split, and they split fairly. The consensus: a first half that's a genuine riot — laugh-out-loud, perfectly paced Priyadarshan farce — followed by a second half that loses the thread. *The Times of India* (3/5) wanted a crisper narrative and a shorter runtime. *India Today* (2.5/5) found the humour dated and the creatures gimmicky. The recurring complaint is the same one Priyadarshan's detractors have leveled for a decade: the man can build a haunted house, but he can't always find the exit.

Here's the thing, though — none of that matters much on a Saturday night with a plate of biryani and a family that grew up on *Bhool Bhulaiyaa*. **Bhooth Bangla** isn't trying to reinvent horror-comedy. It's trying to give you the comfortable, chaotic, slightly-too-long Priyadarshan you remember, with Akshay doing the wide-eyed double-takes that made him a star. On that promise, it delivers.

Stream it for the nostalgia, stay for Tabu and Paresh Rawal turning even thin material into gold, and forgive the climax the way you forgive an old friend who talks too long. It's on Netflix now. The brides may be in danger, but your weekend plans are safe.
